sections.text: In this capstone we build a small text adventure: rooms you walk between, a key to find, and a locked vault to open. A real game would read what you type. This app has no keyboard input, so the commands come from a list in main instead.

The pieces: a Command enum, so the game works with proper values instead of strings. Rooms stored in a HashMap, so we can look one up by name. And a State enum, which makes the game a state machine: it is always in exactly one State, and commands move it from one to another. The Game struct holds the rooms, where you are, what you carry and the state. Its step method takes one Command, changes the game, and returns the text to show. Option<&'static str> means "maybe some text"; &'static str is text that stays valid for the whole program, such as a string literal written straight into the code.

Walk through step, one arm at a time. Look reads the current room and mentions an item if there is one. Go finds the exit for that direction, refuses if the vault is locked, and otherwise moves you (entering the vault sets the state to Won). Take moves the room's item into your inventory, and Unknown answers anything parse did not recognise. In the script (see the Output comment), the first go west fails (locked), then the player fetches the key and the second go west wins.

To grow the game, add a room in Game::new. A new Command variant makes the compiler point at every match that must handle it, but a new word for an existing command needs an arm in parse by hand: parse sends unknown words to Unknown, and the compiler cannot warn about that.
Why use enums here instead of strings everywhere? A string like "go wset" can hide a typo. A Command::Go(Direction::West) cannot be misspelled, and match makes you handle every case.

This is a state machine in the type-driven style: Command models input, State models the phase, and match forces every case to be handled. A typo in a room name is still a runtime panic; an enum RoomId would make it a compile error.

exercise.prompt: In this small parser, parse only knows look. Teach it the word inventory, and also the short form i, so that both give Command::Inventory. The program should print three lines: You see a dusty hall., You carry: key, lamp, I don't understand 'dance'. Hint: in a match, a | b matches either a or b, so the arm can be "inventory" | "i" => Command::Inventory.
exercise.expectedOutput:
You see a dusty hall.
You carry: key, lamp
I don't understand 'dance'.

quiz.question: Why are the rooms stored in a HashMap?
options: HashMap keeps the rooms sorted by name, so the game can print them in order
A room can be looked up quickly by its name, such as "hall" or "vault"
A Vec cannot hold structs, so rooms need a different collection

quiz.question: In parse, what does the last arm _ => Command::Unknown(...) do?
options: Catches every input that no earlier arm matched and keeps the text
Matches only the empty string and ends the game with an error
Stops the whole program with a panic when the player types a word it does not know

quiz.question: What does the State enum model?
options: The list of every room the player has already visited
The text that the player typed at the most recent prompt, kept for the next turn
The phase the game is in: exactly one of Playing or Won at a time
